<div class="exercise" id="exercise-1">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{0}\setcounter{theorem}{2}\setcounter{exercise}{0}
\begin{exercise}
\label{exer:polyregular-marked-squaring-compression} Show that marked squaring is not   compatible with compression, as defined in~\cref{exer:rational-compression}.
\end{exercise}
{{< /latex >}}
<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{0}\setcounter{theorem}{2}
\noindent\textbf{Solution.}\quad Suppose that the input to marked squaring is the string $a^{2^n}$, which has a grammar compression of size linear in $n$. We will show that the output of marked squaring has now grammar compression of size subexponential in $n$. The crucial claim observation is that distances between consecutive underlines in the output of marked squaring will have exponentially many values, while a grammar can only produce a linear number of such distances.
\begin{claim}
    Consider a grammar compression of a string $w \in \set{a,b}^*$. Then 
    \begin{align*}
    \setbuild{ i \in \set{0,1,\ldots}}{$w$ contains an infix of the form $b a^i b$}
    \end{align*}
    has size at most linear in the size of the grammar compression of $w$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}
    Each rule in the grammer can add at most one new value of $i$.
\end{proof}
{{< /latex >}}
</div>
</details>
</div>
<div class="exercise" id="exercise-2">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{0}\setcounter{theorem}{3}\setcounter{exercise}{1}
\begin{exercise}
\label{exer:polyregular-unmarked-squaring} Suppose that we replace marked squaring with the (unmarked) squaring operation from \cref{exer:squaring-continuous}. Show that the resulting class of functions  is a strict subset of the polyregular functions.
\end{exercise}
{{< /latex >}}
<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
{{< latex preamble="book" align="justify" last-line-penalty="1000000" color-map="transducer-book-color-map" >}}
\setcounter{mypart}{4}\setcounter{section}{0}\setcounter{theorem}{3}
\noindent\textbf{Solution.}\quad (Unmarked) squaring is compatible with compression, which is easy to see. Therefore, the resulting class would be compatible with compression, while polyregular functions are not, by \cref{exer:polyregular-marked-squaring-compression}. The result would continue to hold if we added map lifting to the closure properties, while still keeping the squaring operation unmarked. This is because map lifting preserves compatibility with compression, as we have shown in the solution to \cref{exer:regular-compression}.
{{< /latex >}}
</div>
</details>
</div>
